title: Ice Cream 1.5L

drivers.name: Price increase to $6.56
drivers.evidence: Sales dropped 54% vs baseline at same price in 2026-09-28 (24 units). Noise-adjusted estimate: x0.54. One observation, so shrink toward 1.0.

adjustment.analysis: Baseline median is 44.4. No event or promotion in target week. Price increased 2.3% to $6.56, which coincided with a 54% drop in sales (24 units) in 2026-09-28 (vs baseline). That week had no promotion or event. The noise-adjusted effect of a $6.56 price is x0.54. No other price spike with data. Supplier delivery warning adds supply risk, but no demand impact noted. Classical uplift model suggests no lift, consistent with no event. No promotion history at this price. Price increase is a clear demand-lowering driver. Use noise-adjusted effect from single data point: x0.54. Shrink toward 1.0 due to low evidence (one observation). Final multiplier shrunk to x0.75. Downside spread widens slightly to reflect uncertainty.

brief:
PRODUCT: Ice Cream 1.5L | category Frozen | Store #12 (Austin, TX)
TARGET WEEK: 2026-11-09 to 2026-11-15 (5 weeks after the last week with sales data)

KNOWN PLAN FOR THE TARGET WEEK:
  events: none
  shelf price: 6.56 (+2.3% vs regular price 6.41)
  planner notes: Supplier warns of a short delivery

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 44.4 | 5%-95%: 14.3 - 72.8 | 10%-90%: 22.3 - 68.7

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-36% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
